The Comptroller-General of the Nigeria Customs Service, Adewale Adeniyi, has called for tighter arms control and increased vigilance ahead of the 2027 general elections, warning that weapons smuggled into the country could end up in the hands of criminal groups and threaten electoral security. He said the seizure of illicit firearms and ammunition remained critical to national security, citing the interception of 844 rifles and 112,500 rounds of ammunition at a bonded terminal in Onne, Rivers State. Adeniyi stated this at the third Distinguished Personality Lecture organised by the TETFUND Centre of Excellence in Security Management, University of Ibadan, held at the Trenchard Hall of the institution, on Tuesday. Speaking on the topic, “Why Customs Matters: Revenue, Security and Nationhood in a borderless world,” the Customs CG called for increased vigilance, adding that the service handed over 1,599 firearms seized between 2018 and 2024 to the National Centre for the Control of Small Arms and Light Weapons. “On June 21, 2024, our officers intercepted 844 rifles and 112,500 rounds of ammunition at a bonded terminal in Onne, Rivers State. They came in a 40-foot container from Türkiye, hidden among dolls, furniture and plumbing fittings. “In February 2025, we handed over 1,599 firearms seized between 2018 and 2024 to the National Centre for the Control of Small Arms and Light Weapons. “A pattern emerges: the large consignments came by sea, in containers, dismantled or hidden among household goods. This is security performed upstream. “Every rifle stopped at the quay is a rifle that never reaches a forest camp, a kidnapping gang or a polling unit. As the 2027 general elections approach, that vigilance matters even more,” he stated. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. Closure is a blunt instrument, while intelligence, data and joint patrols with our neighbours are sharper ones,” he explained. The Customs boss maintained that the revenue which customs generated helped the government to fulfil its social contract with the people. “Revenue, then, is the material base of the social contract and not just money. A nation that cannot fund itself cannot govern itself. That is the first reason Customs matters. “Customs revenue matters more in developing economies than in rich ones. In 2023, Africa’s average tax-to-GDP ratio was 16.1 per cent, against 33.9 per cent in the OECD. “Large informal sectors make income tax hard to collect. Imports, by contrast, pass through a few points we can watch: seaports, airports and border posts. “This is why trade integration must be pursued with our eyes open, since many countries that cut trade taxes never replaced the lost revenue. “It is also why waivers deserve scrutiny. Import concessions were worth about N1.68 trillion in 2024, and in August, I called for a review of the waiver regime alongside the Customs Act.” Adeniyi, who described the revenue target for 2026 (N11.07 trillion) as demanding, added that the Customs would “pursue the target through compliance, data and facilitation, not through harassment at the ports, because a target met by choking trade would be a false victory.” The Director of TECESM, Prof Benjamin Aluko, described the lecture as “one of the strategies to strengthen the accomplishment of the mandate of our centre in particular and to deepen town and gown collaboration towards solving security-related issues in our society in general.” Aluko noted that the lecture was expected to provide “raw materials and evidence-based data that will drive robust intellectual engagement in security management and peace studies in particular and in social sciences in general.” The lecturer featured a public presentation of a 54-chapter book titled: Perspectives on Security Management in Nigeria, edited by Prof Isaac Albert, Prof Benjamin Aluko and Lt Gen Tukur Buratai (retd.)
